lessons.title: ICT and Its Devices
lessons.notes_html:
What is ICT?

ICT stands for Information and Communication Technology. It is an umbrella term that includes all the computing tools and communication devices — such as computers, cell phones, television, satellite systems and the internet — that let people share information in the digital world. We use ICT to study through distance learning and video lessons, to talk through calls and video conferencing, to work and run businesses, and to get information quickly from anywhere.

Data and Information

Data is a raw collection of facts and figures which has no proper meaning by itself, for example the marks of students written as 45, 67, 89. When this data is processed and arranged in a meaningful form, it becomes information, for example a result card showing that a student passed with 89 marks in Mathematics. So data is the raw input and information is the useful processed output.

Devices of ICT

Five common ICT devices are the computer, smart phone, television, scanner and printer. Other ICT devices include tablets, digital cameras, GPS devices and radios. All these devices are used to create, store, process and communicate information.

Functions of Some ICT Devices

  • Printer (output device): produces a hard copy of documents and pictures on paper.
  • Keyboard (input device): enters data and instructions by typing letters, numbers and symbols; it also has function keys, cursor control keys and a numeric keypad.
  • Scanner (input device): converts hard copy documents and photographs into digital form so they can be edited, saved, printed or shared by email.
  • Monitor (output device): also called a visual display unit; it displays text, pictures and videos — whatever we type or draw appears on its screen.
  • Smart phone: combines a mobile phone with a small computer; it is used for calls and messages, the internet, photos and videos, online learning, GPS navigation and many useful apps.

lessons.title: Hardware, Software and the CPU
lessons.notes_html:
Basic Components of a Computer

The basic components of a computer are: (1) Input devices, used to enter data, (2) Output devices, used to display the result, (3) Memory Unit, which stores data and instructions, (4) Control Unit, which controls all operations, and (5) Arithmetic and Logical Unit (ALU), which performs calculations and logical decisions. Together these parts accept data, process it and produce information.

Why the CPU is Called the Brain

The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is called the brain of the computer because, like the human brain, it controls and directs every activity of the computer. It receives data and instructions, performs all calculations and logical decisions through its ALU, and controls the working of all other parts through its Control Unit. No task in a computer can be done without the CPU.

What is Software?

A set of instructions given to a computer to perform a specific task is called software. Software cannot be touched; it only tells the hardware what to do. This unit discusses three types of software.

Three Types of Software

  • System software: designed to run the computer's hardware and provide a platform for other programs. The operating system is its best example.
  • Application software: performs specific tasks for the user, such as MS Word for documents, MS Office, web browsers and image editors.
  • Driver software (device driver): controls the devices and peripherals connected to the computer, such as printers, scanners and game controllers, and enables them to perform their specific tasks.

Hardware and Software

HardwareSoftware
The physical and tangible parts of a computer that can be seen and touched, e.g. monitor, keyboard, mouse, CPU, printer.A set of instructions, data or programs that cannot be touched; it tells the computer how to function, e.g. Windows, MS Office, games.

Hardware and software are mutually dependent: hardware is useless without software, and software cannot run without hardware. Both must work together to produce a useful output.

lessons.title: Generations of Computers
lessons.notes_html:
First Generation

First generation computers used vacuum tubes. They were very large in size, slow in speed and produced a lot of heat, and they were mainly used for scientific and military calculations. Three well-known computers of the first generation are ENIAC, UNIVAC and EDVAC. Charles Babbage is called the father of the computer.

Second and Third Generations

Second generation computers (about 1956–1963) used transistors instead of vacuum tubes, so they were smaller, faster, cheaper and produced less heat than first generation machines. Third generation computers (about 1964–1971) used Integrated Circuits (ICs), in which many transistors were placed on a single small chip. As a result they became even smaller, more reliable and faster, and able to run many programs, while second generation computers were comparatively bigger and slower.

Fifth Generation

The fifth generation of computers is based on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and very large scale chips (ULSI). These computers can learn from experience, understand natural human language, recognise voices and images, and take decisions like experts. Examples include robots, expert systems, voice assistants and modern smart devices. Their goal is to make computers that can think and reason like humans.

lessons.title: Uses and Effects of ICT
lessons.notes_html:
ICT in Business

In business, ICT devices make work faster, cheaper and more accurate. Computers are used for design, manufacturing, research and development, accounts and record keeping. The internet helps in online buying and selling, advertising and collecting customer feedback. ICT also improves decision making, increases productivity, improves customer services and helps a business compete in the market.

ICT in Manufacturing Industries

ICT devices have revolutionised the manufacturing industry. Robots and computer-controlled machines are used for welding car parts, paint spraying cars, manufacturing microchips, lifting heavy parts of cars, packing goods into boxes, CPU manufacturing, 3D printing and even washing cars. This has increased productivity, improved the quality of products and saved production time, because machines can work continuously with accuracy.

Navigation Systems

Navigation systems are used for monitoring and controlling the movement of a craft or vehicle from one place to another. They are used in land navigation (cars and trains), marine navigation (ships), aeronautic navigation (aeroplanes) and space navigation (spacecraft). The system works with the help of satellites (GPS): the device receives signals from satellites, finds its exact location on the Earth, and then guides the driver or pilot along the correct route on a digital map.

Advantages of ICT

  • ICT is eco-friendly because it has reduced the use of paper.
  • It has improved teaching and learning through online classes and digital material.
  • It has automated manual processes, so work is done quickly and with fewer mistakes.
  • It connects students, teachers and researchers all over the world.
  • It provides independent learning platforms, so a student can learn at his own pace from home.

Disadvantages of ICT

  • Misleading and wrong information can spread easily.
  • There is a risk of cyber-attacks and hacking.
  • Traditional book reading and handwriting habits are decreasing.
  • Managing online courses can be difficult for teachers.
  • ICT devices are not accessible everywhere; implementation is expensive and expert persons are needed to handle them.

lessons.title: Input Devices
lessons.notes_html:
What are Input Devices?

Input devices are the devices used to enter data and instructions into a computer. Data entered through them is converted into a form the computer can understand and process. Examples are the keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, joystick, light pen, digital camera and barcode reader.

The Keyboard

The keyboard is the most common and popular input device. It is used to input text, numbers and commands by pressing keys, and its layout is like that of a traditional typewriter with additional keys for special functions. It has typewriter keys, function keys (F1–F12), cursor control keys and a numeric keypad. Keyboards with 84, 101/102, 104 or 108 keys are commonly available.

Mouse and Joystick

A mouse is a pointing input device that moves the cursor on the screen and is used to select, click, drag and draw objects; it is used with almost every computer. A joystick is also a pointing device with a stick that moves in all directions, but it is mainly used for playing games and controlling machines and simulators.

Light Pen, Scanner and Barcode Reader

A light pen is a pen-shaped input device with a light-sensitive element called a photocell at its tip. When the pen touches the screen, the photocell senses the light and finds the exact position, so the user can draw, write or select objects directly on the screen. A scanner converts a hard copy document or photograph into digital form; we use it to save paper documents safely, edit pictures, send documents by email and make soft copies of old photographs and certificates. A barcode reader is used in shops: it throws a light beam on the barcode printed on a product and senses the reflected light; the pattern of black lines is converted into numbers, and the computer finds the name and price of the product instantly and prepares the bill. OCR stands for Optical Character Reader.

Sensors

Sensors are special input devices that detect changes in the environment, such as light, heat, sound, pressure, motion and temperature, and send this information to a computer or machine. Types of sensors include sound sensors, pressure sensors and light sensors. We use sensors in smart phones, automatic doors, weather stations, fire alarms, cars, robots and scientific experiments. They help machines respond automatically to their surroundings without human help.

lessons.title: Output Devices and Monitors
lessons.notes_html:
Output Devices

Devices that are used to display the result of processing are called output devices. Examples are the monitor, printer and speakers. The most important output device is the monitor, because whatever work we do on the computer is first seen on its screen.

The Monitor

A monitor is an output device that displays the result of processing on its screen in the form of text, pictures and videos; it is also called a Visual Display Unit (VDU). Types of monitors include LCD (Liquid Crystal Display), TFT (Thin Film Transistor), SMD and LED monitors. Modern flat panel monitors are thin, light and use less electricity.

Flat Panel and SMD Monitors

Flat panel monitors are thin and light display screens, such as LCD and LED monitors, which take less space and consume less power. SMD (Surface Mounted Device) monitors use small light-emitting diodes mounted closely on the screen surface, giving brighter colours and sharper pictures, and are often used for large outdoor displays. Both are modern display technologies, but SMD screens are specially known for brightness and large-size display boards.

lessons.title: The CPU and Memory
lessons.notes_html:
The CPU and Its Parts

The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the main part of the computer and is called its brain. It has three main parts:

  • ALU (Arithmetic and Logical Unit): performs all arithmetic operations like addition and subtraction, and logical operations like comparing two values (greater than, less than, equal to).
  • CU (Control Unit): controls and coordinates the working of all parts. It fetches instructions from memory, decodes them, and sends signals to the ALU, memory and input/output devices so every part does its work at the right time — like a traffic controller or manager of the whole system.
  • MU (Memory Unit): stores data, instructions and results during processing.

How a Computer Works — the IPO Cycle

A computer works in three steps. Step 1 — Input: data is entered through input devices like keyboard and mouse. Step 2 — Processing: the CPU processes the data according to the instructions; the ALU calculates and the Control Unit manages the process, while memory stores data temporarily. Step 3 — Output: the processed result, which is information, is shown through output devices like the monitor or printer, and can be saved in storage for future use.

Primary Memory and Secondary Storage

Primary memory (RAM and ROM) is the main memory inside the computer which is directly used by the CPU. It is fast but small in capacity, and RAM loses its data when the computer is switched off. Secondary storage (hard disk, SSD, USB, CD/DVD) stores data and programs permanently in large quantity; it is slower than primary memory but keeps data safe even when the computer is off.

RAM and ROM

RAMROM
Random Access Memory — temporary working memory. Stores the data and programs the CPU is currently using so they can be accessed quickly. We can read and write in it, and everything is erased when the power is off.Read Only Memory — permanent memory. Stores the start-up (boot) instructions of the computer. Its data is not erased when the power is off, and normally we can only read it, not change it.

HDD and SSD

An HDD (Hard Disk Drive) permanently stores the operating system, software, files and documents in large quantity inside the computer. An SSD (Solid State Drive) does the same job but is better than an HDD because it has no moving parts, so it is much faster, silent and more durable; a computer with an SSD starts quickly and opens programs in less time, and it is not easily damaged by shocks.

Can a Computer Work Without Secondary Storage?

A computer can start and do small temporary work without secondary storage, because programs can run in RAM. But it cannot work properly for real use, because RAM is temporary: as soon as the computer is switched off, all data and programs are lost. Secondary storage is needed to permanently save the operating system, software, files and documents, so in practice a computer cannot be used usefully without it.

mcqs.why: Programs can run in RAM temporarily, but RAM loses all data when the computer is switched off; the operating system, software and files must be saved permanently in secondary storage.

lessons.title: System Software
lessons.notes_html:
What is Software?

Software is a set of instructions, data and programs that are used to operate a computer and perform a specific task. It cannot be touched; it only tells the hardware what to do. Software is of two main types: system software and application software.

System Software and Its Types

System software is designed to control and manage the computer's internal and external resources and to run the computer hardware. It works as the primary interface between the hardware and the user applications. Without system software, a computer cannot start or work at all. There are four basic types of system software:

  • Operating System: manages all operations of the computer.
  • Device Drivers: control hardware devices such as printers and scanners.
  • Utility Programs: maintain and protect the system, for example antivirus programs and disk cleanup tools.
  • Language Translators: convert programs into machine language.

Operating Systems

Microsoft Windows is the most commonly used operating system for personal computers. It provides a graphical desktop with icons, windows, taskbar and start menu, and supports almost all kinds of software. Android is an operating system for mobile phones and tablets, developed by Google; it is touch-based and runs millions of apps. Other examples are macOS, Linux and iOS.

Functions of an Operating System

  • It starts the computer and manages its hardware.
  • It provides a user interface (desktop, icons, windows) so we can use the computer easily.
  • It manages files and folders — creating, naming, saving, copying and deleting them.
  • It runs and manages application programs, often many at the same time.
  • It controls input/output devices and memory.
  • It provides security through user accounts and passwords.

Utility Software and Device Drivers

Utility software helps to maintain, protect and improve the working of the whole computer, for example antivirus programs. A device driver has the specific job of controlling a particular hardware device, such as a printer, scanner or mouse, and letting it communicate with the computer. In short, utilities look after the whole system, while drivers look after individual devices.

Language Translators

Language translators are system software that convert programs written in a programming language into machine language which the computer understands. The main types are: (1) Assembler — converts assembly language into machine code. (2) Compiler — converts a high-level language program into machine code all at once. (3) Interpreter — converts and executes a high-level language program line by line.

mcqs.why: Utilities look after the whole system (antivirus, disk cleanup), while drivers look after individual devices such as a printer or scanner.

lessons.title: Application Software
lessons.notes_html:
What is Application Software?

Application software refers to programs written to carry out a certain task of the user, such as writing text, making calculations, editing images or browsing the internet. It always runs with the help of the operating system. Its main types are:

  • Productivity software (MS Word, Excel, PowerPoint)
  • Educational software (learning and teaching programs)
  • Entertainment software (games, music and video players)
  • Web browsers (Chrome, Firefox)
  • Graphics software (Paint, Paint 3D, Photoshop)

Productivity Software

Productivity software is application software used to produce information in the form of documents, presentations, spreadsheets and databases. Examples include MS Word for documents, MS PowerPoint for presentations, MS Excel for calculations and MS Access for databases. It is called productivity software because it helps offices, schools and businesses complete their daily work quickly and neatly.

Educational Software

Educational software is application software designed for teaching and learning. Teachers use it to prepare lessons, presentations and tests, and students use it to learn subjects through lessons, quizzes, videos and practice exercises. Examples include typing tutors, learning apps and encyclopaedias. It makes learning interesting, visual and easy, and students can learn at their own speed.

Web Browsers

A web browser is application software that opens web pages and allows us to view information from the internet. We type the address of a website in the browser, and it brings the page from the internet and displays it on the screen. Moving from one web page to another through links is called browsing or surfing. Famous web browsers are Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge, Opera and Safari. Browsers also let us use search engines, watch videos, attend online classes and use social and educational websites.

Search Engines

A search engine is a website that allows us to search for information on the internet. We type words about the topic, and it shows a list of related web pages within seconds. Two famous search engines are: (1) Google — the most widely used search engine, known for fast and accurate results. (2) Bing — Microsoft's search engine, which gives search results along with pictures and news. Other examples are Yahoo and DuckDuckGo. To search: open the browser, go to the search engine, type the specific words, press Enter, view the results and click the most relevant link.

lessons.title: Steps of Problem Solving
lessons.notes_html:
The Problem Solving Process

Problem solving follows a systematic, step-by-step process:

  • Problem Identification: clearly defining what the problem actually is — what is given (facts/input) and what result is required (output). It is the first and most important step; when the problem is identified correctly, we do not waste time on wrong solutions.
  • Problem Analysis: the process of defining and decomposing a problem — studying it deeply, collecting important facts, ignoring irrelevant material and breaking it into smaller sub-problems.
  • Planning the Solution: deciding the steps (algorithm) before actually solving. A good plan arranges all steps in the right order, so mistakes are found on paper before real work starts and the risk of failure is greatly reduced.
  • Selecting the Best Solution: comparing possible solutions and choosing the best one, considering correctness, time, cost and resources, simplicity and efficiency.
  • Implementing and Testing the Solution: applying the solution and checking whether it works; if not, improving the plan and trying again.

Benefits of the Step-by-Step Process

  • The problem becomes clear and easy to understand.
  • No important point is missed, so the chance of failure decreases.
  • Big problems can be divided and solved in small parts.
  • Time and resources are saved because work is done in proper order.
  • The solution can be tested and improved easily at each step.

Simple and Complex Problems

A simple problem is small, clear and can be solved in a few easy steps with one clear answer, for example making a cup of tea or adding two numbers. A complex problem is big, has many parts and conditions, and needs to be broken into sub-problems and solved step by step, for example arranging a school function or building a computer program. Complex problems need proper planning, while simple problems do not.

Problem Solving in Everyday Life

We face small and big problems daily — planning a journey, managing pocket money, repairing a bicycle, preparing for exams or cooking a meal — and all need the same steps: identify the problem, analyse it, plan, act and check the result. People who solve problems step by step make fewer mistakes, save time and money, and stay confident instead of becoming worried.

lessons.title: Computational Thinking
lessons.notes_html:
Deconstruction of a Problem

Deconstruction (decomposition) of a problem means breaking down a big, difficult problem into smaller and simpler sub-problems, solving each sub-problem separately, and then joining their solutions to solve the main problem. Its benefits are: the problem becomes easy to understand; each part can be solved and tested separately; different people can work on different parts; mistakes can be found and fixed in a small part without disturbing the whole solution; and the same sub-solutions can be reused in other problems.

Techniques of Deconstruction

  • Identifying what is given (facts and input) and what output is required.
  • Dividing the main problem into smaller sub-problems.
  • Pattern identification — looking for similarities among the sub-problems.
  • Abstraction — ignoring irrelevant material and keeping only the important information.
  • Solving each sub-problem and then integrating (joining) the sub-solutions.

Pattern Recognition and Abstraction

Pattern recognition (pattern identification) means looking for similarities and common features among problems or within the parts of a problem. If we have already solved a similar problem, the same method can be used again, which saves time. Abstraction means thinking about the important part of the problem and ignoring irrelevant material.

Computational Thinking

Computational thinking helps us solve a problem in a logical, computer-like way. It has four main parts: decomposition — breaking the problem into smaller parts; pattern recognition — finding similarities with known problems; abstraction — focusing only on important information; and algorithmic thinking — writing a clear sequence of steps for the solution. Its benefits are that big problems become manageable, solutions can be reused, and it improves logical thinking and confidence in decision making in everyday life.

lessons.title: Algorithms and Flow
lessons.notes_html:
What is an Algorithm?

An algorithm is a finite sequence of instructions to solve a specific problem. Every algorithm has a start and a stop. Algorithms must use specific instructions — clear, exact and complete instructions that can be followed in only one way, for example 'Add 2 and 3'. Nonspecific instructions are vague and incomplete, for example 'Add some numbers', which different people may follow differently, so they cannot be used in an algorithm.

Three Types of Flow

  • Sequential flow: steps are executed in the same sequence in which they are written.
  • Conditional flow: steps are executed only if a certain condition is true; if the condition is false, those steps are skipped or another set is followed, for example 'If it is raining, take an umbrella'.
  • Repetitive flow (loop): a set of statements is executed again and again until a certain condition is met, for example 'Keep adding water until the glass is full'. Conditional flow is about choosing, while repetitive flow is about repeating.

Example Algorithms from the Book

Sum and average of three numbers: 1. Start. 2. Input three numbers A, B and C. 3. Sum = A + B + C. 4. Average = Sum / 3. 5. Display Sum and Average. 6. Stop. Example: for 6, 9 and 12, Sum = 27 and Average = 27 / 3 = 9.

Even or odd: 1. Start. 2. Input a number N. 3. Divide N by 2 and find the remainder. 4. If the remainder is 0, display 'N is Even'. 5. Otherwise display 'N is Odd'. 6. Stop. This algorithm uses a conditional statement: 14 gives remainder 0, so 14 is even; 9 gives remainder 1, so 9 is odd.

Product of two numbers — choosing the best algorithm: Algorithm 1 (direct multiplication): Product = A x B in one step. Algorithm 2 (repeated addition): add A, B times. Algorithm 1 is better because it is shorter, faster and works in one step for all numbers, while Algorithm 2 needs many repetitions when B is large.

Table of a number: uses repetition — a counter goes from 1 to 10, each time Result = N x Counter is displayed, until the counter passes 10.

lessons.title: Programs and Programming Languages
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Program?

A program is a set of instructions that is used by the computer to perform a specific task. The function of a program is to instruct the computer: the computer follows the instructions step by step to take input, process it and produce the required output. Without a program, a computer cannot do any useful work.

Programming Languages

A programming language is a language used to write instructions (code) for a computer so that it can solve a problem or perform a task. Just as we use Urdu or English to communicate with people, we use a programming language to communicate with the computer. Every programming language has its own rules, called syntax. Examples are machine language, assembly language, C, Python and Scratch. A value that remains consistent (does not change) during the execution of a program is called a constant, while a value that can change is stored in a variable.

Three Types of Programming Language

  • Machine language: the lowest level language, written in binary (0 and 1), which the computer understands directly without any translator. It is the fastest but the hardest for humans.
  • Assembly language: a low-level language that uses short words (mnemonics) instead of binary. The programmer who uses it requires a translator — an assembler — to convert the assembly language program into machine language. It is a little easier than machine language but machine-dependent.
  • High-level language: uses English-like words and is easy for humans to write, for example C and Python. It needs a compiler or interpreter for translation, and it can be used on different computers.

lessons.notes_html:
What is Scratch?

Scratch is a visual programming language and software that makes it easy to create interactive games, animations and stories. Instead of typing commands, we join colourful blocks together like a puzzle to make programs. Scratch is specially designed for beginners and students to learn programming concepts in a fun way.

Sprite, Stage and Script Area

The character in Scratch is called a Sprite. The Stage is the area where we see the result of the program — the sprites move, speak and act on the stage, like actors on a theatre stage. The Script Area is the working area where we create the program by joining blocks together for a sprite. In short, we write the program in the script area and watch its output on the stage. A previously saved program can be opened from the File menu.

Block Categories in Scratch

  • Motion: enables the Sprite to move (move steps, go to a position, bounce if on edge).
  • Looks: makes the Sprite say things and change colour or costume.
  • Sound: has the blocks to play sounds.
  • Sensing: has the blocks to allow the Sprite to ask questions and to help the Sprite detect its environment.
  • Control: has the blocks to control the flow of instructions (forever, if-then, repeat).
  • Operators: blocks for calculations, joining text and random numbers.
  • Events: blocks that start the program, such as 'when green flag clicked' or 'when space key pressed'.

Example Scratch Programs from the Book

Bouncing ball: use 'when space key pressed' (Events), add 'forever' (Control), and inside it 'move 10 steps' and 'if on edge, bounce' (Motion). The ball then moves on its own and bounces back from the boundaries. Multiplication game: the sprite welcomes the user, sets two variables to random numbers from 1 to 12, asks their product using Sensing, and if the answer is correct it changes colour and displays 'Well done' — using events, variables, random numbers, sensing and conditional blocks together.

lessons.notes_html:
What is Debugging?

Debugging is the process of testing the software to find and eliminate the errors (bugs) in it. A program may fail or give wrong output because of a wrong block, a wrong value or a wrong order of instructions; debugging locates and removes such errors.

Strategies of Debugging

  • Forward analysis: reading the program step by step from the start to find where the error occurs.
  • Backward analysis: starting from the point where the failure message appears and tracing the program backward from the location of the failure message in order to identify the region of faulty code.
  • Testing the program with different inputs and checking the output.
  • Fix and validate: fixing the error and testing again to confirm the program now works correctly.

Steps of Debugging

  • Step 1 — Identify the error: run the program and note where and when it fails or gives wrong output.
  • Step 2 — Locate the faulty code: use forward or backward analysis to find the exact instructions causing the problem.
  • Step 3 — Understand the cause: decide why the error happened (wrong block, wrong value or wrong order).
  • Step 4 — Fix the error: correct the code.
  • Step 5 — Test and validate: run the program again several times to confirm the error is removed and no new error has appeared.

lessons.title: Citizens and Digital Citizens
lessons.notes_html:
Citizenship

Citizenship is the status of being a member (citizen) of a community or country. A citizen enjoys certain rights and privileges given by the nation, and in return he must obey the country's laws, respect the rights of others and defend the country against its enemies. For example, we live in Pakistan, therefore we are citizens of Pakistan.

Responsibilities of a Citizen

The responsibilities of a citizen are: to be honest and trustworthy; to follow rules and laws; to respect the rights of others; to practice tolerance; to be informed about the world around him; to respect the property of others; to be compassionate; to take responsibility for his actions; and to pay taxes. A citizen must comply with all of these.

Digital Citizenship

A person who develops the skills to effectively use the internet and other digital technology is called a digital citizen. Digital citizenship is the ability of a citizen to safely and responsibly access digital technologies while being an active and respectful member of society. Responsible digital citizenship also means behaving lawfully, protecting your privacy and that of others, and recognising your rights.

Basic Elements of Digital Citizenship

  • Safe and responsible use of technology.
  • Respectful and lawful behaviour online.
  • Protecting personal information and privacy.
  • Giving credit to the owners of online work (avoiding plagiarism and piracy).
  • Balanced and healthy use of devices, including proper posture and taking breaks.
  • Being a positive and active member of the online community.

Importance of Digital Citizenship

Digital citizenship is important because today we study, communicate, shop and work through digital technology. A good digital citizen uses technology safely, lawfully and respectfully, so the online world remains safe for everyone. It protects us from dangers like hacking, fraud, cyber-bullying and harmful content, protects the rights of creators through copyright, and builds our good image (digital footprint), which matters for our future education and jobs.

lessons.title: Lab Rules, Safety and Health
lessons.notes_html:
Rules of the Computer Lab

  • No food or drinks inside the lab.
  • Save your work often.
  • Do not go on unapproved sites.
  • Handle the keyboard, mouse and other equipment gently and carefully.
  • Keep the lab neat and do not change the settings of computers without the teacher's permission.

Note that using the printer in the lab (with permission, for your work) is allowed — 'Do not use printer in lab' is NOT a computer lab rule.

Rules for Being Safe and Responsible Online

  • Never share personal information (address, school, passwords) with strangers.
  • Use strong passwords and do not share them.
  • Do not download files from unknown websites.
  • Be respectful in comments and messages; do not bully anyone.
  • Give credit when you use someone else's work.
  • If something makes you feel unsafe or uncomfortable, tell a trusted adult immediately.

NO-GO-TELL

One of the key strategies when feeling unsafe or uncomfortable, whether online or offline, is to approach a trusted adult. The NO-GO-TELL approach means: (1) Say NO when someone is making you feel uncomfortable or unsafe. (2) Then GO: leave or run away from that person or situation. (3) And TELL: talk to a trusted adult (parent or teacher) about the situation.

Proper Posture and Health Issues

Proper posture: sit straight with your back supported by the chair, feet flat on the floor, screen at eye level about 50 cm away from the eyes, elbows bent at about 90 degrees and wrists straight while typing. To reduce strain, follow the 20-20-20 rule (after every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds), blink often, and take a short break and stretch after every 30–40 minutes. By excessive use of ICT devices we can face health issues: eye strain and weak eyesight; back and neck ache from wrong posture; Repetitive Strain Injury (RSI), such as carpal tunnel syndrome in the wrist, from typing and using the mouse for long periods; headache and disturbed sleep; and less physical activity leading to weakness and obesity.

lessons.title: Copyright, Plagiarism and Piracy
lessons.notes_html:
Copyright

Copyright is a type of intellectual property right that protects the original works of an owner, such as books, computer programs, films, music and pictures. It gives the owner the legal right to copy, publish and sell his work, and no other person can reproduce or use it without permission. If someone copies it illegally, it is piracy and the owner can take legal action. In this way copyright encourages people to create new work without fear of theft.

Plagiarism and Its Types

Plagiarism is presenting someone else's work or ideas as your own, with or without consent. It is an offence because it is a kind of theft and dishonesty: the real creator loses the credit and reward of his hard work, and the plagiarist gets marks or fame for work he did not do. In schools and universities it leads to punishment, cancellation of work and loss of trust. Its types are:

  • Global plagiarism: plagiarizing an entire text and presenting it as your own.
  • Patchwork plagiarism: copying phrases and ideas from different sources and joining them together.
  • Self plagiarism: recycling your own previous work and submitting it again as new.
  • Paraphrasing plagiarism: changing a few words of someone's text without giving credit to the source.

Piracy

Piracy is the act of illegally reproducing copyrighted material, such as books, computer programs and films, without the permission of its owner. Downloading paid software, songs or movies free from illegal websites and selling copied CDs are examples of piracy. Piracy causes heavy loss to the creators and companies and is a punishable crime.

Ethics of Sourcing Online Information

Ethical issues while surfing online include plagiarism, piracy, spreading false information, abusive language or bullying, invading someone's privacy and visiting harmful websites. The ethical standards of sourcing online information are: always mention the name of the author and the website; do not copy large parts of text word for word — read, understand and write in your own words; take permission for pictures and other copyrighted material, or use free material; check that the information is from a reliable source; and never present downloaded assignments or projects as your own work.

lessons.title: Entrepreneur and Entrepreneurship
lessons.notes_html:
Who is an Entrepreneur?

An entrepreneur is an individual who initiates a new business and bears most of the risks associated with it and enjoys most of the rewards. He starts a business venture and is responsible for its development. An entrepreneur is also commonly known as an innovator who sources new ideas, goods, services and business procedures.

What is Entrepreneurship?

Entrepreneurship is the process of setting up a business. It means identifying a need or opportunity, arranging resources, starting a new venture and running it successfully while taking risks. Entrepreneurship creates new products and services, provides jobs to people and plays a vital role in the economy of a country and its development.

Why is an Entrepreneur a Risk Taker?

An entrepreneur is called a risk taker because he invests his own money, time and effort in a new business whose success is not guaranteed. The business may earn profit or may fail and result in losses. The entrepreneur bears most of these risks himself and still starts the venture with courage and planning. If the entrepreneurship proves successful in taking on the risks of creating a startup, it is rewarded with profits, fame and continued growth opportunities.

How Entrepreneurship Develops an Economy

  • It creates new businesses and new jobs, reducing unemployment.
  • It brings new and better products and services to the market.
  • It increases competition, which improves quality and lowers prices.
  • Entrepreneurs pay taxes which the government uses for development.
  • Successful businesses earn fame and profit for the country through trade.

Famous Entrepreneurs

Two famous entrepreneurs are Bill Gates, co-founder of Microsoft, who made personal computers and Windows software popular all over the world, and Steve Jobs, co-founder of Apple, famous for the iPhone and other innovative products. Other examples are Elon Musk (Tesla, SpaceX) and Muhammad Yunus of Bangladesh, who introduced microfinance through Grameen Bank and helped millions of poor people start small businesses.

lessons.title: Types of Entrepreneurship
lessons.notes_html:
Traditional and Digital Entrepreneurship

Traditional entrepreneurship is based on a physical business, such as a shop or factory, which needs a proper place, serves mostly local customers and works for fixed hours. Digital entrepreneurship runs through the internet and digital technology, for example an online store or a mobile app; a digital online business does not require a physical existence, can serve customers all over the world at any time, and usually has less or no overhead costs. Digital businesses can also grow (scale) much faster than traditional ones. There are 9 types of entrepreneurship in total.

Small Business and Large Company Entrepreneurship

In small business entrepreneurship, a person owns and runs his own small business, such as a local grocery store, hairdressing salon, small boutique or plumbing service, usually hiring local or family employees; its aim is a profit that supports the family and a modest lifestyle. Large company entrepreneurship is found in big established companies run by advanced professionals and teams of executives, which keep creating new products and services according to market demand, for example Microsoft, Google and Disney. A small business can turn into large company entrepreneurship when it grows rapidly or is acquired by a large company.

Some Kinds of Entrepreneurs

Imitators are entrepreneurs who use others' business ideas as inspiration but work towards improving them. Researcher entrepreneurs take their good time when starting their own business, as they want to have complete knowledge of the product before offering it. Hustlers work very hard and are willing to work their way up. Technology has enabled business owners and leaders to stay on top of their projects by tracking time and progress.

E-commerce and the Traditional System

E-commerceTraditional System
Buying and selling goods and services through the internet: the customer selects products on a website or app, pays online or on delivery, and receives goods at home. It is open all the time and everywhere, and an e-business generally has less or no overhead costs.Buying and selling at a physical shop or market: the customer visits personally, sees the goods and pays in cash during fixed shop hours. It is limited to a place and time.

Steps of the Entrepreneurial Process

  • Discovery: identifying a business opportunity or a problem to solve.
  • Planning: making a business plan about the product, customers, resources and money needed.
  • Resourcing: arranging capital, people and material.
  • Developing / Launching: starting the business and offering the product or service.
  • Managing and growing: running the business successfully, earning profit and expanding it.

An entrepreneur who succeeds in this process is rewarded with profits, fame and continued growth opportunities. In a class project, a good business plan states the idea, the investment needed, the expected income, the risks and their solutions — for example an online home tutoring service has almost no overhead cost and can grow from one town to the whole district.

Why Digital Entrepreneurship is Preferred Nowadays

  • It does not require a physical shop or office, so starting costs and overhead costs are very low.
  • It can reach customers all over the world through the internet, 24 hours a day.
  • Technology helps owners track time, progress and sales easily.
  • Hiring a virtual assistant can give your business smart tech solutions with a human touch.
  • A successful digital business can grow and scale much faster than a traditional business.
